abstract_sentences.text: This paper proposes asymmetric perturbation, where only one player's payoff function is perturbed, for solving bilinear saddle-point optimization problems, commonly arising in minimax problems, game theory, and constrained optimization.
Symmetric perturbation is known to require decreasing its strength to ensure convergence to a solution, i.e., an equilibrium in the original game, resulting in a slower rate.
comparisons: symmetric perturbation versus the target original game
abstract_sentences.transition: contrasts the baseline before the new idea.

abstract_sentences.text: First, with asymmetric perturbation, we show that, for a sufficiently small perturbation strength, the equilibrium strategy of the asymmetrically perturbed game coincides with an equilibrium strategy of the original unperturbed game.
qualifiers: for a sufficiently small perturbation strength
comparisons: asymmetrically perturbed game versus original unperturbed game

abstract_sentences.text: Second, building on this coincidence, we construct a learning algorithm with a linear last-iterate convergence rate.
abstract_sentences.transition: turns the invariance into an algorithmic rate.

abstract_sentences.text: Third, motivated by the fact that the coincidence relies on the perturbation strength being sufficiently small, we also provide a parameter-free variant, retaining the linear rate.

evidence.anchor: parameter-free variant, retaining the linear rate

abstract_sentences.text: Finally, we empirically demonstrate fast convergence toward equilibria in both normal-form and extensive-form games.

abstract_analysis.strongest_claim_location: Sentence 3, PDF p. 1: exact coincidence with an original-game equilibrium strategy.

method_analysis.formal_objects: Bilinear A, polytope strategy spaces X/Y, profile z, equilibrium sets X*/Y*, game value v*, and NashConv are introduced on PDF p. 2.
method_analysis.components_to_problems: One-sided quadratic perturbation addresses fixed symmetric bias; alternating projected updates operationalize it; adaptive halving removes unknown alpha; dilated regularization makes sequence-form updates efficient.
method_analysis.algorithm_detail: Algorithm 1 takes epsilon, initial eta/mu and strategies; an outer episode halves mu, while two inner player-specific GDA solvers stop at a gap threshold before a NashConv test.
method_analysis.algorithm_invariants: mu_k is halved and eta_k is non-increasing by the update rule; the two role-specific solvers are combined only at the outer stopping test.
method_analysis.method_figures_tables: No flowchart or method table. Figure 2 is a mechanism diagram and Figure 3 is an update trajectory.

final_judgment.single_storyline: One-sided quadratic perturbation preserves an original minimax strategy below a game-dependent threshold, making a stable perturbed dynamic useful for the original bilinear game (PDF p. 4).
final_judgment.main_body_keeps: The main body keeps the objective, invariance theorem/corollary, update, rate statements, proof sketch, normal-form trajectory, five-game figure, and explicit limitations (PDF pp. 3-9).
final_judgment.appendix_moves: Complete proofs, Algorithm 1, seed protocol, tuned hyperparameters, sensitivity, CFR comparison, and the arbitrarily-small-threshold construction move to Appendix A-K (PDF pp. 12-35).
final_judgment.best_pattern: Figures 1-2 establish a counterintuitive phenomenon and mechanism before Theorem 3.1/Corollary 3.2, then Figure 3 and Figure 4 connect the update to two empirical regimes.
final_judgment.largest_gap: Extensive-form AsymP-DGDA has no corresponding convergence theorem, Figure 4 has no reported uncertainty/repetition details, and the allowable threshold can be arbitrarily small (PDF pp. 6, 8-9, 17-18).
final_judgment.transfer_rule: When a stabilizing regularizer may bias the target solution, test whether an asymmetric placement preserves the original solution set and state the threshold explicitly before claiming an algorithmic rate.
final_judgment.transfer_boundary: The rule needs a proved solution-set growth or error-bound structure. This paper proves it only for bilinear polytope two-player zero-sum games, not dilated dynamics or Markov games.
